questions.question: What is a ResultSet in JDBC and how do you iterate it?
questions.title: JDBC ResultSet — Iterating Query Results
questions.direct_answer: **ResultSet** holds the results of a SQL SELECT query. It is a cursor positioned before the first row. Call `rs.next()` to advance to the next row (returns false when no more rows). Read column values using `rs.getString(colName)`, `rs.getInt(colIndex)`, etc.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic ResultSet iteration and column reading
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that cursor starts before first row — must call rs.next() before reading
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention both column name and column index approaches, and explain that column names are preferred for readability

sections.title: ResultSet Iteration
Key Points
sections.content:
- ResultSet cursor starts BEFORE the first row
- rs.next(): moves to next row, returns true if row exists
- Column names: rs.getString("name") — readable, resilient to column order changes
- Column index: rs.getString(1) — slightly faster, breaks if column order changes
- rs.wasNull(): check if the last read value was NULL
- Default ResultSet: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY, CONCUR_READ_ONLY (cursor only moves forward)
- Always close ResultSet explicitly or use try-with-resources

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A ResultSet is a cursor-based object that holds the results of a SELECT query. The cursor starts positioned before the first row. You call rs.next() in a while loop — each call advances the cursor to the next row and returns true if a row exists, or false if all rows have been processed. Within each iteration, you read column values using typed getter methods like rs.getString for text, rs.getInt for integers, rs.getDouble for decimals. You can reference columns by name using the column name string, which is more readable and resilient to changes in column order, or by 1-based index position. Always close the ResultSet when done — use try-with-resources.

beats.text: A ResultSet is a database cursor that holds the rows returned by a SELECT query. It starts positioned before the first row. Each call to rs.next() moves the cursor forward by one row and returns true if that row exists, or false when there are no more rows.
Using a cursor means rows are streamed from the database rather than loaded all at once. For large results, this avoids loading millions of rows into memory.

items: Before-first position — cursor starts here; reading before calling next() gives nothing
rs.next() — advances to next row, returns true if a row exists
Typed getters by name — rs.getLong('id'), rs.getBigDecimal('total'); preferred for readability
Typed getters by index — rs.getLong(1); slightly faster but breaks if column order changes
After-last position — rs.next() returns false here; the loop ends

beats.text: Fetching orders: executeQuery returns a ResultSet. The while loop calls rs.next() — first call moves to row 1, returns true. rs.getLong('id') reads the id column, rs.getBigDecimal('total') reads the total. Next iteration moves to row 2. When all rows are processed, rs.next() returns false and the loop exits. try-with-resources closes the ResultSet. items: Reading a column before the first rs.next() call — you'll get a 'cursor is before the first row' exception.
Using column index 1 when the SELECT * column order might change — always prefer column names for stability.

speakable_v2.cap: ResultSet is a cursor, not a list. Call rs.next() before every read, and close it when done.

questions.question: How do you check for NULL values when reading from a ResultSet?
questions.title: Checking NULL Values in JDBC ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: For primitive getter methods (getInt, getDouble), JDBC returns 0 for NULL — use `rs.wasNull()` after reading to check if the value was actually NULL. For String-returning `rs.getString()`, it returns Java null directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: NULL handling in ResultSet primitive types
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that getInt returns 0 for NULL and not checking wasNull()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between Object getters (getString returns null) vs primitive getters (getInt returns 0 for null)

sections.title: NULL Handling in ResultSet
Key Points
sections.content:
- getString, getObject: return Java null for SQL NULL
- getInt, getLong, getDouble, getBoolean: return 0/false for SQL NULL
- rs.wasNull(): call immediately after getter to check if last value was NULL
- Use getObject() for nullable numeric columns to get null instead of 0
- After rs.wasNull() is called, it only reports the most recently read column
- Checking wasNull is important for financial data where 0 vs NULL matters

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: NULL handling in ResultSet depends on the getter method type. For String-based methods like getString, JDBC returns Java null when the database column is SQL NULL. But for primitive-type methods like getInt, getLong, getDouble, JDBC returns zero for SQL NULL because Java primitives cannot represent null. If you need to distinguish between a genuine zero value and null in an int column, call rs.wasNull() immediately after the getter — it returns true if the last read value was NULL in the database. A cleaner alternative is to use getObject for nullable numeric columns, which returns a proper Java Integer or null.

Primitive getters like getInt return 0 (and getBoolean returns false). To detect the difference, call rs.wasNull() immediately after a primitive getter.

For a cleaner approach: Integer discount = (Integer) rs.getObject('discount') returns null directly without needing wasNull(). speakable_v2.cap: For nullable numeric columns, either call wasNull() right after getInt, or use getObject with a cast. getString handles NULL safely without extra steps.

questions.question: What is ResultSet TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY vs TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE?
questions.title: ResultSet Types — Forward-Only vs Scrollable
questions.direct_answer: **TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY** (default): cursor can only move forward with next(). **TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE**: cursor can move in any direction using previous(), absolute(), relative(). Scrollable ResultSets are slower and less common — most use cases only need forward iteration.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to call previous() on a TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY ResultSet
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that scrollable ResultSets buffer more data and that most production code uses forward-only

rows: Any direction; does not see DB changes

sections.title: Creating Scrollable ResultSet
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: By default, a ResultSet is TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY, meaning you can only call next() to advance the cursor one row at a time in the forward direction. If you need to navigate backwards or jump to specific rows, you can create a scrollable ResultSet by passing TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE as a parameter to prepareStatement. This allows methods like previous(), first(), last(), and absolute(n) to jump to any row. However, scrollable ResultSets are slower because the driver needs to buffer more data, and they are rarely needed in practice. For most applications, forward-only is the right choice.

groups.heading: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY (default)
groups.text: The cursor can only move forward with rs.next(). Rows are streamed from the database one at a time. This is memory-efficient and the fastest option. It's the right choice for nearly all production queries.

groups.heading: TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE
groups.text: The cursor can move in any direction: next(), previous(), first(), last(), absolute(n). The driver buffers all rows in memory to enable this. It gives you a snapshot of the data at query time and doesn't reflect subsequent DB changes.

items: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY — default; use for every normal query; stream rows and process them once.
TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE — only when you genuinely need backward navigation or random row access; avoid for large result sets.

beats.text: Reading the orders table: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY streams rows as you iterate. To count total rows, you'd need rs.last() to jump to the last row and rs.getRow() — but that requires TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE and buffers everything. Better approach: use a COUNT(*) query instead.

speakable_v2.cap: Stick with forward-only in production. Scrollable ResultSets buffer all rows and are rarely worth the memory cost.

questions.question: How do you map ResultSet rows to Java objects in JDBC?
questions.title: Mapping ResultSet to Java Objects in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: Map ResultSet rows to Java objects manually: iterate with `rs.next()`, read each column with typed getters, set values on a Java object. This is verbose but gives full control. Spring's JdbcTemplate with RowMapper simplifies this significantly.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how to map multiple rows into a List of objects
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both manual mapping and mention Spring JdbcTemplate RowMapper as a cleaner alternative

sections.title: ResultSet to Object Mapping
Key Points
sections.content:
- Manual mapping: verbose but transparent and full control
- Create a new object per row, set fields from ResultSet
- Use ArrayList to collect multiple rows
- Spring JdbcTemplate: RowMapper lambda for cleaner mapping
- JPA/Hibernate: ORM handles this automatically with entity classes
- Column names in ResultSet match SQL aliases if you use AS

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In plain JDBC, you map ResultSet rows to Java objects manually. You iterate with while rs.next, create a new Java object for each row, call the typed getter methods to read each column, set the values on the object using setters, and add the object to a list. This works but is verbose for tables with many columns. Spring's JdbcTemplate simplifies this with a RowMapper — you provide a lambda that takes a ResultSet row and returns an object, and JdbcTemplate handles the iteration and resource management. JPA and Hibernate take this further by eliminating manual mapping entirely through object-relational mapping annotations.

questions.question: What happens if you do not close a ResultSet in JDBC?
questions.title: Consequences of Not Closing ResultSet in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: Not closing a ResultSet leaks the **cursor resource** on the database server. Each unclosed ResultSet consumes server memory. Additionally, if the Connection or Statement is closed first, the ResultSet is closed too — but relying on this is bad practice.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming closing Connection is enough and not explicitly closing ResultSet
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that databases have cursor limits and too many open cursors cause ORA-01000 (Oracle) or similar errors

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Unclosed ResultSet: server-side cursor remains open, consuming resources
- Databases have cursor limits: ORA-01000 (Oracle max open cursors exceeded)
- Closing Statement closes ResultSet automatically
- Closing Connection closes Statement (and ResultSet) automatically
- BUT: do not rely on this chain — explicitly close all resources
- try-with-resources: closes in declared order (ResultSet first, then Statement, then Connection)

sections.title: Proper Resource Closing Order
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Not closing a ResultSet leaves an open server-side cursor consuming database resources. Databases have a limit on the number of open cursors per session or globally. If you accumulate too many unclosed ResultSets, you will hit this limit and get errors like ORA-01000 on Oracle or similar on MySQL. Technically, closing the Statement will close the ResultSet, and closing the Connection will close all associated Statements and ResultSets. But relying on this implicit chain is bad practice — you should explicitly close the ResultSet. The cleanest approach is try-with-resources which handles closing automatically even when exceptions occur.

beats.text: Every open ResultSet holds a server-side cursor that consumes database memory and counts against the server's open cursor limit. Failing to close it means that cursor stays open until the connection is eventually closed or the database times it out.
ResultSet is not just a Java object — it corresponds to a live cursor tracked by the database server. Closing it tells the server to free that cursor's resources.

items: Unclosed ResultSet — server cursor stays open; memory consumed on the DB server
Cursor limit hit — Oracle throws ORA-01000 (maximum open cursors exceeded); MySQL has a similar limit
Implicit close chain — closing Statement closes its ResultSets; closing Connection closes its Statements; but don't rely on this
try-with-resources — closes ResultSet, then Statement, then Connection in reverse declaration order automatically

beats.text: If a method fetches orders but an exception escapes before closing the ResultSet, the server cursor remains open. Repeat this under load and 100 leaked cursors consume memory and eventually trigger a 'max open cursors exceeded' error. try-with-resources on the ResultSet declaration guarantees the cursor is released regardless of exceptions. [depth: how Oracle's ORA-01000 cursor limit applies per session vs globally and how to check open cursor count with v$open_cursor]

items: Relying on Connection.close() to clean up ResultSets — that works eventually, but the cursor is open the whole time the connection is alive.
Using JPA and thinking this doesn't apply — Hibernate opens JDBC ResultSets internally; it closes them but misconfigured lazy loading can leave them open.

speakable_v2.cap: Always close ResultSets explicitly. try-with-resources is the safest one-line way to guarantee it.

questions.question: What is ResultSetMetaData and how do you use it?
questions.title: ResultSetMetaData Usage
questions.direct_answer: ResultSetMetaData provides information about a ResultSet's columns at runtime: column count, column names, data types, and nullability. You get it from rs.getMetaData() and use it to inspect query results without knowing the schema ahead of time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of JDBC's runtime introspection capabilities
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using hardcoded column names/indices instead of using metadata for generic result processing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ORMs and frameworks like JdbcTemplate use ResultSetMetaData internally for their RowMapper implementations

sections.title: Using ResultSetMetaData
Key Points
sections.content:
- Get with: ResultSetMetaData meta = rs.getMetaData()
- getColumnCount(): how many columns in the result
- getColumnName(i): column name at position i (1-indexed)
- getColumnTypeName(i): SQL type as string
- Useful for generic result processing (building dynamic maps, CSV export)
- Spring's ColumnMapRowMapper uses ResultSetMetaData to build Map<String, Object>
- ORM frameworks use it internally for entity mapping

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ResultSetMetaData gives you runtime information about the columns in a ResultSet — the column count, names, SQL types, and nullability. You get it by calling rs.getMetaData() after executing a query. It's particularly useful when you're building generic utilities that don't know the query's schema in advance — for example, a CSV exporter that needs to dynamically write headers, or a debug tool that prints any query result as a table. You iterate from column 1 to getColumnCount() and call getColumnName(i) for the header and rs.getObject(i) for each value. In practice you rarely write this code yourself. Spring's JdbcTemplate uses ColumnMapRowMapper which internally uses ResultSetMetaData to convert each result row into a Map of column name to value. Hibernate and other ORMs also use it to map query results to entity fields. Knowing it exists is useful for debugging or building data tooling.

questions.question: What is a scrollable ResultSet and when would you use one?
questions.title: Scrollable ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: A scrollable ResultSet allows forward and backward navigation through results, plus absolute positioning. Created with ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE or TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE. Rarely used in modern apps — pagination SQL is almost always preferred.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of ResultSet types beyond the default forward-only
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Loading all rows into a scrollable ResultSet when SQL LIMIT/OFFSET pagination would be far more efficient
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE and TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE and why forward-only is the default

sections.title: ResultSet Types
sections.content:
**Three ResultSet types:**

| Type | Navigation | Sees DB changes? |
|---|---|---|
| TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY (default) | Forward only | No |
| TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE | Any direction | No (snapshot at query time) |
| TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE | Any direction | Yes (live view) |

**Creating a scrollable ResultSet:**
```java
Statement stmt = conn.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY);
ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);

rs.last();  // move to last row
int rowCount = rs.getRow(); // total rows
rs.absolute(5); // jump to row 5
rs.previous(); // move backward
rs.first();  // back to start
```

**Why forward-only is the default:**
- Cursor-based: database sends rows as you call next() — memory efficient
- No need to buffer all rows
- Scrollable requires buffering entire result set in memory

**Modern alternative:** Use SQL LIMIT/OFFSET for pagination — far more efficient

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Default ResultSet is TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY — only next() works
- TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE: random access, snapshot of data at query time
- TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE: random access, reflects concurrent DB changes
- Scrollable ResultSet buffers all rows in memory — avoid for large result sets
- Methods: absolute(n), relative(n), first(), last(), previous()
- Modern preference: paginate with SQL LIMIT/OFFSET instead of scrollable ResultSet

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: By default, a JDBC ResultSet is forward-only — you can only move through rows using next(), and you can never go backward. A scrollable ResultSet, created with TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE or TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE, allows you to move freely: forward with next(), backward with previous(), jump to a specific row with absolute(n), or jump to last() to count rows. TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE gives you a snapshot of the data at query time. TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE reflects changes made by other transactions, though this is rarely used in practice. The main downside of scrollable ResultSets is memory: the driver must buffer all rows. For forward-only, rows can be streamed from the database one at a time. In modern applications, I'd almost never use a scrollable ResultSet for pagination. SQL's LIMIT and OFFSET or keyset pagination is far more efficient because the database only retrieves the rows you need. Scrollable ResultSets are more of a legacy feature that you might encounter in older codebases.

questions.question: How do you handle null values in a JDBC ResultSet?
questions.title: Handling Nulls in ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: After calling getInt() or getDouble() on a null column, JDBC returns 0 (not null). Call rs.wasNull() immediately after to check if the last value read was actually null. For reference types like getString(), null is returned directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Edge case awareness — null handling is a common source of bugs in JDBC code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating getInt() returning 0 as the actual value without checking wasNull()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the wasNull() pattern and mention using getObject() with a type cast as an alternative for nullable primitives

sections.title: Null Handling in ResultSet
Key Points
sections.content:
- Primitive getters (getInt, getDouble) return 0/false for NULL — not null
- Call rs.wasNull() immediately after a primitive getter to detect SQL NULL
- wasNull() refers to the most recently read column — order matters
- String and Object getters return Java null for SQL NULL
- Alternative: rs.getObject("age") returns Integer (boxed) or null
- This is a common source of bugs when 0 is a valid value but NULL means missing

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Null handling in JDBC is a subtle but important detail. For reference types like getString() or getObject(), JDBC returns Java null when the database column is NULL — straightforward. The problem is with primitive getters like getInt() and getDouble(). Java primitives can't be null, so JDBC returns 0 for a null integer and false for a null boolean. If 0 is a valid value in your business logic, you can't distinguish between an actual 0 and a missing value just from getInt()'s return value. The solution is rs.wasNull(), which you call immediately after the getter. It returns true if the last column read was SQL NULL. You must call it right after because it refers to the most recently read column. An alternative I prefer for nullable numeric columns is rs.getObject() with a cast to the wrapper type — getObject on a null integer column returns Java null, letting you use Integer instead of int and check for null naturally.

speakable_v2.hook: JDBC returns 0 for a NULL integer column. That's the same as a real zero. wasNull() or getObject() is how you tell the difference.

beats.text: When a column contains SQL NULL, JDBC's primitive getters (getInt, getLong, getDouble, getBoolean) return 0 or false because Java primitives can't be null. Object getters (getString, getObject) return Java null. The wasNull() method lets you check whether the last value read was actually NULL.
The Java type system doesn't allow primitives to be null. JDBC has to return something from getInt on a NULL column, so it returns 0 and provides wasNull() as a separate null-detection mechanism.

items: getString / getObject — return Java null for SQL NULL; no extra step needed
getInt / getLong / getDouble / getBoolean — return 0 or false for SQL NULL; use wasNull() to distinguish
rs.wasNull() — returns true if the last column read was NULL; must be called immediately after the getter
getObject(column) with cast to Integer — returns null for SQL NULL; avoids the wasNull dance

beats.text: Reading a nullable order discount column: int discount = rs.getInt('discount') returns 0. rs.wasNull() tells you whether that 0 was an actual zero discount or a missing value. Alternatively, Integer discount = (Integer) rs.getObject('discount') returns null directly for a NULL column, letting standard null-check code handle it. For a financial system where zero means 'no discount' and NULL means 'discount not yet applied', the distinction matters. [depth: why rs.wasNull() reports only the most recently read column and why order-of-calls matters]

items: Reading a second column between getInt and wasNull() — wasNull() now reports the second column's null status, not the first.
Using a primitive int field in a JPA entity for a nullable database column — Hibernate stores 0 when null is expected; use Integer wrapper instead.
